title: What actually happens when you leave a Trading Bot (EA) running for 16 months?
author: CommandantZ
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I've been professionally developing trading robots, mostly MT5 Expert Advisors, and other financial systems for around 7 years now. I also trade with the bots I develop, and have been running a few of them for multiple years. During that time, I've learned a few things about automated trading that I thought I'd share here.

The first thing I've learned is to... avoid compounding profits (yeah I'm actually not kidding). When I develop an EA, I generally aim for relatively high returns, usually between 6% and 14% a month (-> see attached pictures). My reasoning is simple: if I'm going to spend months developing a system that targets 10% a year, I might as well invest in the S&P 500 instead. Of course, aiming for higher returns means accepting higher risk. My systems usually stay below 10% drawdown, but I've experienced occasional spikes reaching 15% or 17%.

For that reason, I prefer withdrawing my profits every month and moving them into more traditional investments, such as index funds. This reduces the returns from compounding, but I find it more reasonable than increasing my exposure to relatively risky strategies.

Another important lesson is that monitoring remains essential. My systems can handle things like scheduled economic announcements and exposure management automatically, but there are still situations where I manually intervene. I've disabled my EAs during major geopolitical events, including the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, the Iran-US war, tariff announcements, or even recently, the midterms. I'm experimenting with using AI to automate some of these decisions.

Something else I've noticed is how much market regimes and luck influence performance. An EA can perform extremely well for several months and then struggle, even though nothing has changed in its code. Some strategies perform better in trending markets, others in ranging markets, and sometimes the sequence of trades simply isn't in your favour.

I've learned to avoid constantly modifying my systems whenever they experience a drawdown. If an EA is still operating within its expected risk parameters, I generally prefer letting it continue (or shutting it down) rather than trying to optimize it after every bad month. Obviously, if its behaviour starts deviating significantly from what I observed during development, that's a different story.

Finally, technical issues are something I believe every EA developer should take seriously. I've been fortunate enough not to experience any major disasters, but I always try to account for scenarios such as broker disconnections, VPS interruptions, or execution errors.

For example, if your EA loses connection while holding open positions, what happens when it reconnects? Does it recognize those positions? Does it accidentally open duplicate trades? Does it know whether it should resume trading? These are things that should be handled directly in the code. A reliable VPS is essential, but proper disaster recovery is just as important.

Overall, I think the biggest lesson from running EAs for several years is that developing a profitable strategy is only part of the job. Capital management, monitoring, adapting to market conditions, and technical reliability all matter just as much. Basically, everything "around the EA" is just as important as the EA itself.

Yeah, extremely pleased with MetaTrader (though of course, there are always some things that could get better, much better). But for algotrading, I do believe it's probably one of the most complete solutions (especially with MQL5). 

Claude and other AIs can indeed generate good MQL5 code, but as I usually say, would you trust putting money into a system that you can't proof check yourself? At the moment, I wouldn't  do so without going through human checks as well, to ensure the produced code reflects my original idea.

replies.body:
this is probably a better question for the entire sub than here but i wonder if there’s any utility to having a bot whose job it is to just buy from xyz stocks as soon as the short moving average crosses over the long term and then just hold them indefinitely until there’s a trend reversal. in other words a bot that more often than not just buys & holds? will metatrader do this?

i apologize so much if im bothering you lol. i feel lost out there not having a platform yet

replies.author: CommandantZ
replies.body:
That's definitely the kind of "basic" EAs that could be developed with MQL5 on MetaTrader. As a matter of fact, you could go into MUCH MUCH more complicated and complex stuff than that. 

But let's take your example for the sake of it, the important question is: how do you define a trend reversal algorithmically? You should remember that bots don't just "see" or "feel" things that we do. It's just numbers for them. You need to find some kind of signal determining a trend reversal. An algorithmic (exact and punctual, formally defined) signal.

comments.author: tampalasan
comments.body:
Woah! That's pretty cool! I'm just starting to explore bot trading with cTrader but I think I need to have a look at MT5 now. 

Based on your experience and your strategies, what is your ideal testing duration (both backtesting and paper trading) to properly validate a trading bot?

replies.author: CommandantZ
replies.body:
cTrader is fine as well, though as it is quite new compared to MT, the eco system is just a bit less developed. 

Aaaah, I do not like that question at all haha! Simply because there is no ideal testing duration, but you need to test intelligently. 

Typically, the longer the better, however, suppose you run your backtest for 20 years, and no luck you end up loosing everything during the 2008 financial crisis. Well in that case, it does not mean your EA is bad or anything, heck, everyone lost in 2008!

Same goes with Covid and others. Do not backtesting on time periods, backtest on market regimes. 

So again, the most important is to always take a step back on your backtesting, and consider the market conditions at time of backtesting. A loosing backtest does not always mean your bot is bad, sometimes it just means your bot wasn't made for those specific market circumstances.

comments.author: trepeatapp
comments.body:
on the reconnect / duplicate trades point, the usual fix is to find your own positions by magic number at startup and on every reconnect, instead of trusting anything kept in memory. what actually causes the duplicates is in-memory state like an "already traded today" flag or a cooldown timer, which resets when the terminal restarts. saving those to global variables or a file fixes most of it

easy to test too: open a position, kill the terminal, reopen it and watch what the EA does

replies.author: CommandantZ
replies.body: Yes... but that's not all. I'm not necessarily speaking about just identifying your positions, that, as you very rightly said, can be done via Magic Number. However, what about the actual trading strategy itself ? What if the disconnect was fairly long, and your setup no longer makes sense (as per your trading strategy), how do you handle trades that, for example, were supposed to be closed or partially closed ? That's the kind of problematic you face.

replies.author: trepeatapp
replies.body:
Fair point, positions are the easy half. The strategy state is the hard one.

What I'd do is save the plan per ticket when the trade opens (partial levels, time exit, whatever the strategy would do next), so on reconnect the EA checks each position against where price is now, not just that it exists. Then a rule decided up front for a missed step: act on it at market, or treat it as gone. And past a certain time offline, no catching up at all. It flags it and waits for you.

For partials specifically, splitting the entry into two positions with their own TPs puts the partial on the broker's server, so a disconnect can't miss it. Hedging accounts only though.

Curious how you handle it in yours. Do you let the EA decide on reconnect, or do you always step in yourself?
